depth.transferChallenge: Change one value, type, or boundary in the sample. Write the exact stdout or diagnostic you expect before asking rustc. Keep the focus on borrowing for read-only access.

writing.exampleCaption: length borrows text, so main can print it again.
writing.explanation:
The & symbol creates a borrow. A shared reference such as &str permits reading but not mutation, and it does not own the value it points to. Passing a reference avoids a move, so the original binding remains usable after the call. Later ownership lessons add the precise aliasing rules and mutable references.

In the example, name owns a String. Passing &name to length creates a shared borrow, and the parameter text: &str lets the function read the bytes through that borrow. length returns a usize, not the text itself. After the call ends, main still owns name and can print it. No second owned String had to be made for this read-only question.

A reference is valid only while the value it refers to is available. Rust checks that relationship so code cannot keep a pointer into a value that has already gone away. Shared references permit reading; mutation through a shared reference is not allowed. That is why a function that only needs to inspect text should often accept &str instead of taking String ownership. It can then work with both owned strings and borrowed string slices supplied by callers.

Borrowing is not a promise that the data will never change anywhere. It is a controlled access rule for a particular period and reference. Later lessons introduce mutable borrows and the rule that prevents conflicting simultaneous access. For now, change length to take String by value and see why the owner is unavailable after the call. Restore &str and explain what the ampersand changed about the function's contract.

References also have lifetimes, although the compiler often infers them in simple cases. A reference cannot outlive the value it points to. Return owned data or borrow from an input that lives long enough; do not try to return a reference to a local temporary.

A reference lets code temporarily use a value without becoming its owner. If a function accepts `&String` or `&str` to read text, the caller retains the original value after the call. The borrow must remain valid while the reference is used, and a shared borrow does not permit mutation of that value through the same reference. This is easier to understand if you draw two names: the owning binding and the temporary reference pointing to it.

Trace the example at the call site: who owns the string before the call, what the function can read, and who owns it afterward. Replace the borrowed parameter with an owned `String` and observe whether the caller can still use its binding. Then restore the reference. Prefer `&str` for a read-only text parameter when both string literals and `String` values should work. The signature says what the function needs; the borrow checker enforces that promise.
